newsitem.title: GHANA: Ghana eyes top U.N. job, rest of Africa restrained.
newsitem.headline: Ghana eyes top U.N. job, rest of Africa restrained.

text.p: Ghana said on Wednesday it was ready to propose its own man for U.N. secretary-general but most African nations held firm behind Boutros Boutros-Ghali or opted for caution or discretion.

There was, however, a surprising silence from the Addis Ababa headquarters of the Organisation of African Unity (OAU), which in July threw its weight behind Boutros-Ghali, whose bid for a second term has run into a U.S. veto.
Ghana's Foreign Minister Obed Asamoah told Reuters that Ghana was ready to propose Ghanaian Under-Secretary-General Kofi Annan, who heads U.N. peacekeeping operations.

"Ghana, along with other members of the Organisation of African Unity, supported the candidature of Boutros-Ghali but with the U.S. veto the door is open for Ghana and other countries to support another candidate," he said by telephone.
"We are prepared to propose and support Mr Kofi Annan."
U.S. Ambassador Madeleine Albright voted against a new five-year term for Egypt's Boutros-Ghali on Tuesday on grounds the U.N. needed someone more amenable to reform.
But Boutros-Ghali's supporters, a majority of U.N. members plus 14 of the powerful Security Council's 15 members, appear to have no intention of giving up without a fight.
The Council has agreed to give priority to candidates from Africa on the grounds that if Boutros-Ghali is denied a second term, he should at least be followed by another African.

The Arab League said the veto could affect U.S. interests in the Arab world. "We regret the American position. This position will not serve well the interests of the United States in Arab states," secretary-general Esmat Abdel Meguid said in Cairo.
Diplomats in New York and elsewhere and other U.N. watchers are juggling with a string of names -- some heavyweights, others less likely candidates at first glance.
The OAU was strangely silent. Although it has repeatedly backed a second term for Boutros-Ghali, the 45-member body had no immediate official comment after the veto.
Diplomats noted that the OAU secretary-general, Salim Ahmed Salim of Tanzania, was widely tipped as a potential successor.

James Jonah, Sierra Leone's U.N. ambassador and a former U.N. under-secretary-general, is another name mentioned. Jonah successfully organised multi-party national elections in his war-ravaged home country early this year.
Hamid Algabid, secretary-general of the Organisation of the Islamic Conference, has been proposed by his native Niger.

A name on some lips is Graca Machel, widow of Mozambique's independence president Samora Machel and close friend of South Africa's Nelson Mandela. She has just concluded a mammoth U.N. report on the Impact of Armed Conflict on Children.
Some African nations were outspoken.

"The United Nations has not done anything tangible for Africa. It is not a serious organisation. We are not concerned about election of the secretary-general right now," Ugandan President Yoweri Museveni told a news conference on Tuesday.
Ivory Coast, the world's top cocoa producer, as many other African nations, has yet to comment officially on the U.S. veto.
Officials said it would work through the OAU but did not rule out presenting an Ivorian candidate if Boutros-Ghali stood down. Foreign Minister Amara Essy's name has been mentioned.

"We still stand on Boutros Boutros-Ghali's candidature being resubmitted," Kenyan Foreign Ministry spokesman David Kikaya said, but he added: "If the view is that (his) candidature is not acceptable, I think we would have to get another consensus from the OAU on another candidate."
